newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House to vote on congressional term limits.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House to vote on congressional term limits.

text.p: Supporters of Congressional term limits disagreed among themselves on Tuesday as they prepared for House votes over proposed constitutional amendments on how long U.S. representatives and senators may serve.

None of the 11 amendments to be considered on Wednesday was likely to get the two-thirds majority needed for passage, but supporters say the votes will increase pressure on opponents to eventually support term limits or risk re-election defeat.
If more than one amendment does get a two-thirds majority, the one with the most votes will be adopted.

"We will get accountability of every member of the House," Representative Bob Inglis, a South Carolina Republcan, told reporters. "About 80 percent of the American people support term limits," but, "We probably have some tough sailing in the House."

Inglis wants to limit House members to three two-year terms and senators to two six-year terms. But the House Judiciary Committee approved an amendment setting 12-year limits for House and Senate members.

Other proposed amendments include several versions that set a six-year House term and a 12-year Senate limit; one with an eight-year House term and 12 years in the Senate; one to let each state set limits for its members of Congress and another that would apply limits to current members.
"If we're for term limits, let's have them immediately," said Representative John Dingell, Democrat of Michigan, who has served for 42 years. "I think the whole idea is silly."
U.S. Term Limits, a private group, angered many term limits proponents by attacking anyone who did not support six-year House and 12-year Senate limits.
"This organisation is dedicated to their way and none other," said Representative Bill McCollum, a Florida Republican, who sponsors the 12-year limit for members of both chambers.
The House last voted on term limits in 1995 as part of the Republican Contract with America, but it fell 63 votes short.
Backers of term limits said they will make members of Congress more responsive to the public by eliminating career lawmakers who gain power through seniority.
Opponents said term limits would force out experienced members and were not needed because voters can remove incumbents at any election.

The U.S. Constitution set House terms at two years and Senate terms at six years, but there was no limit on how often members may run for re-election. Presidents have been limited to two four-year terms since passage of an amendment in 1951.
